PROPOSITION 209: CONSTITUTIONAL BAR ON PREFERENCES IN PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for City of Springfield · Associate Governmental Program Analyst

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California Constitution Article I, Section 31 -- the provision added by Proposition 209 (1996) that bars the state and its political subdivisions from discriminating against, or granting preferential treatment to, any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in the operation of public employment. It concerns a hiring decision by City of Springfield regarding the position of Associate Governmental Program Analyst, potentially involving the applicant Jordan T. Reyes. It states facts about what the constitutional text itself says -- the prohibition, which entities it covers, its stated exceptions, its remedies provision, and its effective-date and severability language. Article I, Section 31 also addresses public education and public contracting; this document focuses on the public-employment application only and does not address the education or contracting contexts. This corpus separately includes documents addressing FEHA-based hiring restrictions such as the Fair Chance Act and the California Fair Pay Act, which apply to different employers (including private employers) under different statutory schemes; this document does not restate those and addresses only the distinct constitutional rule that applies to public employers. It is not itself a job posting, an offer, or any notice, and it does not tell City of Springfield or Jordan T. Reyes what to do about any particular hiring decision.

THE CORE PROHIBITION: NO DISCRIMINATION OR PREFERENTIAL TREATMENT IN PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT
California Constitution Article I, Section 31, subdivision (a) states that the State shall not discriminate against, or grant preferential treatment to, any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in the operation of public employment (the same sentence also names public education and public contracting as covered activities). The provision was added to the California Constitution by Proposition 209, an initiative measure approved by voters on November 5, 1996.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "The State shall not discriminate against, or grant preferential treatment to, any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in the operation of public employment, public education, or public contracting."
  — Cal. Const. art. I, § 31, subd. (a) (California Legislative Information text), California Constitution, Article I, Section 31, subdivision (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2031.&article=I)
  Known gap: The constitutional text does not itself define "discriminate," "preferential treatment," or "the operation of public employment," and does not itemize which specific personnel decisions (recruitment, testing, hiring, promotion, layoff, or other decisions) fall within "the operation of" public employment. This document quotes the text of subdivision (a) as written; it does not attempt to summarize the substantial body of published California case law interpreting the scope of that language, because case-law research for this document could not be completed -- CourtListener's search tool returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, "Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") on every attempt made while drafting this document, and no case citations are included here as a result. A reader relying on this document should not assume the absence of case citations means no relevant case law exists.

WHICH PUBLIC EMPLOYERS ARE COVERED: THE DEFINITION OF "STATE"
Article I, Section 31 defines "State" broadly for purposes of the section. The definition names the State itself, along with any city, county, city and county, public university system (including the University of California), community college district, or school district, and it adds special districts and "any other political subdivision or governmental instrumentality of or within the State" as covered entities as well. The statutory phrase "but not necessarily be limited to" signals that the named list of entities is illustrative rather than a closed, exhaustive list.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "For the purposes of this section, “State” shall include, but not necessarily be limited to, the State itself, any city, county, city and county, public university system, including the University of California, community college district, school district,
special district, or any other political subdivision or governmental instrumentality of or within the State."
  — Cal. Const. art. I, § 31, subd. (f) (California Legislative Information text), California Constitution, Article I, Section 31, subdivision (f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2031.&article=I)
  Known gap: The California Legislative Information HTML for this subdivision contains a mid-sentence line break in the source markup between "school district," and "special district" (confirmed by inspecting the raw fetched HTML, where the text node itself contains a literal newline character at that point, not a rendering artifact introduced afterward); this document treats that as a source-formatting line wrap and quotes the sentence with the line break preserved rather than silently removing it. Separately, the subdivision does not define "governmental instrumentality," so this document cannot state with precision where the outer boundary of coverage lies for an entity that is not on the named list -- for example, a joint powers authority or a quasi-public corporation created by statute.

EXCEPTION FOR BONA FIDE SEX QUALIFICATIONS
Article I, Section 31 states that nothing in the section is to be interpreted as prohibiting bona fide qualifications based on sex that are reasonably necessary to the normal operation of public employment (the same sentence also names public education and public contracting). The provision does not create a parallel exception for bona fide qualifications based on race, color, ethnicity, or national origin -- the exception as written is limited to sex.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "Nothing in this section shall be
interpreted as prohibiting bona fide qualifications based on sex which are reasonably necessary to the normal operation of public employment, public education, or public contracting."
  — Cal. Const. art. I, § 31, subd. (c) (California Legislative Information text), California Constitution, Article I, Section 31, subdivision (c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2031.&article=I)
  Known gap: The California Legislative Information HTML for this subdivision contains a mid-sentence line break in the source markup between "shall be" and "interpreted" (confirmed by inspecting the raw fetched HTML, where the text node itself contains a literal newline character at that point); this document treats that as a source-formatting line wrap and quotes the sentence with the line break preserved. The constitutional text does not itself define "bona fide qualifications" or "reasonably necessary," and this document does not attempt to state how those terms have been applied to any specific job classification or qualification standard, because the case-law research needed to do so could not be completed (see the gap disclosure on the core-prohibition clause in this document, describing the CourtListener rate-limit error encountered while drafting).

EXCEPTIONS: PRE-EXISTING COURT ORDERS AND FEDERAL PROGRAM ELIGIBILITY
Article I, Section 31 states two further exceptions. First, nothing in the section is to be interpreted as invalidating any court order or consent decree that was already in force as of the section's effective date. Second, nothing in the section is to be interpreted as prohibiting action that must be taken to establish or maintain eligibility for a federal program, where ineligibility would result in a loss of federal funds to the State.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "Nothing in this section shall be interpreted as invalidating any court order or consent decree which is in force as of the effective date of this section."
  — Cal. Const. art. I, § 31, subd. (d) (California Legislative Information text), California Constitution, Article I, Section 31, subdivision (d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2031.&article=I)
  "Nothing in this section shall be interpreted as prohibiting action which must be taken to establish or maintain eligibility for any federal program, where ineligibility would result in a loss of federal funds to the State."
  — Cal. Const. art. I, § 31, subd. (e) (California Legislative Information text), California Constitution, Article I, Section 31, subdivision (e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2031.&article=I)
  Known gap: The text does not state a mechanism for identifying which court orders or consent decrees were "in force as of the effective date" (November 5, 1996), and does not address what happens when such an order or decree is later modified, extended, or expires. It also does not name which federal programs the federal-funding exception might apply to, or specify what showing an entity would need to make to invoke it; this document does not attempt to supply that missing detail.

REMEDIES AVAILABLE FOR A VIOLATION
Article I, Section 31 states that the remedies available for a violation of the section are the same, regardless of the injured party's race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin, as the remedies that are otherwise available for violations of then-existing California antidiscrimination law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "The remedies available for violations of this section shall be the same, regardless of the injured party’s race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin, as are otherwise available for violations of then-existing California antidiscrimination law."
  — Cal. Const. art. I, § 31, subd. (g) (California Legislative Information text), California Constitution, Article I, Section 31, subdivision (g) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2031.&article=I)
  Known gap: The provision defines the remedy by cross-reference to "then-existing California antidiscrimination law" rather than stating a remedy directly, and it does not identify which antidiscrimination statutes or common-law causes of action that cross-reference points to, or how a court is to select among them when more than one might apply. This document does not attempt to trace that cross-reference to any specific antidiscrimination statute's remedial provisions.

PROSPECTIVE EFFECT, SELF-EXECUTING NATURE, AND SEVERABILITY
Article I, Section 31, subdivision (b) states that the section applies only to action taken after the section's effective date. Subdivision (h) states that the section is self-executing, that if any part of the section is found to be in conflict with federal law or the United States Constitution the section is to be implemented to the maximum extent that federal law and the United States Constitution permit, and that any provision held invalid is severable from the remaining portions of the section. The California Legislative Information text carries a history note stating that Section 31 was added on November 5, 1996, by Proposition 209, an initiative measure.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "This section shall apply only to action taken after the section’s effective date."
  — Cal. Const. art. I, § 31, subd. (b) (California Legislative Information text), California Constitution, Article I, Section 31, subdivision (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2031.&article=I)
  "This section shall be self-executing. If any part or parts of this section are found to be in conflict with federal law or the United States Constitution, the section shall be implemented to the maximum extent that federal law and the United States Constitution permit. Any provision held invalid shall be severable from the remaining portions of this section. (Sec. 31 added Nov. 5, 1996, by Prop. 209. Initiative measure.)"
  — Cal. Const. art. I, § 31, subd. (h), history note (California Legislative Information text), California Constitution, Article I, Section 31, subdivision (h), and enactment history note (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2031.&article=I)
  Known gap: The text does not itself state the calendar date on which the section's "effective date" fell (as distinct from the November 5, 1996 election date on which the initiative was approved) -- for a voter initiative, the effective date and the election date are not necessarily the identical calendar day, and this document does not resolve that distinction. This document also does not summarize any published decision addressing a federal-law or federal-constitutional conflict under subdivision (h), for the case-law-access reason disclosed in the gap field of the core-prohibition clause in this document.
